# Contributor handoff: option values and resource ownership

Scope: the supplied Click checkout, commit `b6c8e841138ac6fe48aafbfe8c145fd5b88dc8ac`.
[Package metadata](pyproject.toml) declares **8.2.1**, Python **>=3.10**.
This is a source review, not a runtime verification. Documentation, implementation,
and repository tests were read; no dependencies were installed or code/tests run.
Links below point to canonical files in this checkout; retain the commit when
comparing behavior with other releases.

## Environment-driven flags

- Value precedence is command line → environment → `Context.default_map` →
  parameter default ([`Parameter.consume_value`](src/click/core.py#L2268)).
  Explicit `envvar` names precede automatic names. An `envvar` list selects the
  first **nonempty** value, not simply the first defined variable; empty values
  fall through. See [environment documentation](docs/options.md),
  [`resolve_envvar_value`](src/click/core.py#L2359), and
  [`test_empty_envvar`](tests/test_options.py#L203).
- **8.2.1 pitfall:** for an explicit environment value, when `is_flag` and
  `flag_value` are truthy, Click substitutes `str(flag_value)` before type
  conversion. Thus a conventional `is_flag=True` option with `envvar="FEATURE"`
  activates even for `FEATURE=false`, `0`, or other nonempty text. Unsetting it
  or setting it empty allows fallback; an explicit CLI choice still wins.
  [`test_envvar_flag_value`](tests/test_arguments.py#L201) demonstrates arbitrary
  text selecting `"upper"`; the boolean consequences follow from
  [the implementation](src/click/core.py#L2961), not a dedicated false-value test.
- The [8.2 changelog](CHANGES.rst#L65) says `flag_value` is “always” used, but the
  implementation qualifies that claim: falsey `flag_value` skips substitution,
  and automatic-prefix lookup returns raw text. Where raw text reaches
  [`BoolParamType`](src/click/types.py#L661), whitespace/case are normalized;
  `1/true/t/yes/y/on` and `0/false/f/no/n/off` are accepted, other text errors.
  Do not apply a generic boolean environment recipe uniformly to these paths.
- For nonboolean flags, `default=True` selects the flag's value, rather than
  passing `True` to the callback ([flag docs](docs/options.md),
  [`Option.get_default`](src/click/core.py#L2912)). 8.2.1 also fixes explicitly
  typed flags; consult [the release notes](CHANGES.rst#L3) and
  [`test_flag_value_is_correctly_set`](tests/test_options.py#L1025) before
  changing type inference.

## Chained commands and cleanup

The group result callback receives the ordered list of subcommand results plus
the group's parameters. Each chained subcommand context closes before that
callback; the **group context remains open through result processing**
([`Group.invoke`](src/click/core.py#L1796)). Therefore a returned processor must
not depend on an already-open file owned by its subcommand's `click.File`.
Keep shared files/resources on the group context, or pass paths and open them
inside the processor for the full duration of consumption. Merely switching to
`open_file` does not arrange ownership or cleanup.

This narrows the broad “file types cannot be accessed” warning in
[pipeline documentation](docs/commands.rst#L269): the same page's group-owned
input file is valid. [`test_pipeline`](tests/test_chain.py#L135) exercises that
pattern, but only asserts output after excluding an abort trailer; it is not
evidence of a clean exit. [`test_no_command_result_callback`](tests/test_chain.py#L89)
covers `invoke_without_command=True`, with an empty result list in chain mode.
[Chaining restrictions](docs/commands.rst#L157): no nested groups, options before
arguments per command, and only the last command may have `nargs=-1`.

Use `ctx.with_resource(manager)` for context managers and `ctx.call_on_close(fn)`
for cleanup callbacks. A local `with` inside a group callback ends too early for
subcommands ([resource guide](docs/advanced.rst#L334)).
[Context implementation](src/click/core.py#L571) uses an `ExitStack`: cleanup is
in reverse registration order; `close()` drains and replaces the stack.
[Context exit](src/click/core.py#L475) closes at the outermost nesting depth
before popping the current context; `scope(cleanup=False)` defers cleanup.
Since 8.2, [`ctx.exit()`](src/click/core.py#L710) explicitly closes resources
before raising `Exit`. Tests cover [normal and early exit](tests/test_context.py#L224),
[eager option callbacks](tests/test_context.py#L284), and
[`with_resource`](tests/test_context.py#L410).
Do not assume exception-aware transactional behavior: `Context.__exit__` calls
`ExitStack.close()` without forwarding the active exception to resources.

## Interactive defaults

Environment values and `default_map` bypass automatic prompting. For an editable
environment-derived suggestion, use `prompt=True` with a callable default such
as `default=lambda: os.environ.get("USER", "")`, as shown in
[dynamic prompt defaults](docs/prompts.rst#L120). A higher-priority environment
binding or map value for that option still bypasses the prompt.
[`Option.consume_value`](src/click/core.py#L2998) is the deciding logic.

`prompt_required=False` prompts on a bare option; omission uses the default.
`required=True` also prompts on omission. See the
[optional prompt tests](tests/test_termui.py#L399).
Use `show_default="current user"` to describe a callable in help
([tests](tests/test_options.py#L319)). Since 8.2, `show_default=False` also hides
the default in the prompt ([test](tests/test_termui.py#L478)); it does not remove
the default itself. Avoid combining `multiple=True` and automatic prompting;
the [prompt guide](docs/prompts.rst) recommends prompting inside the callback.

## CliRunner compatibility

In 8.2+, `result.stdout` and `result.stderr` are independent; `result.output`
contains the combined stream in capture order. Empty stderr is `""`, without an
exception. `mix_stderr` was removed. Assert `stdout` for machine output and
`stderr` for diagnostics; use `output` when the combined transcript matters.
Text properties decode with replacement and normalize CRLF; the corresponding
`*_bytes` properties preserve captured bytes. See
[`Result` and `CliRunner`](src/click/testing.py#L165) and
[`test_stderr`](tests/test_testing.py#L344).

8.2.1 flushes stderr at invocation end ([regression test](tests/test_testing.py#L455))
and fixes stdin EOF handling ([release notes](CHANGES.rst#L3)).
Prompts echo supplied input unless hidden. The runner mutates global interpreter
state and is not thread-safe ([testing guide](docs/testing.md)). That guide's
“Context Settings” example asserts a debug message its callback never emits;
use it for the `terminal_width` mechanism, not that output expectation.

## File opening

- `click.File` registers cleanup with the parsing context; an already supplied
  file-like object is returned unchanged. `click.Path` validates/returns a path
  without opening it ([file guide](docs/handling-files.rst),
  [`File.convert`](src/click/types.py#L771)).
- The guide describes writes as lazy, but
  [`File.resolve_lazy_flag`](src/click/types.py#L762) defaults to lazy only when
  the mode contains `w`, excluding `-`; append/exclusive modes are not implicitly
  lazy. `click.open_file` defaults to **`lazy=False`** and requires caller-managed
  lifetime ([implementation](src/click/utils.py#L358)). Lazy reads still perform
  an initial open/close validation; later open failures raise `FileError`
  ([`LazyFile`](src/click/utils.py#L109)).
- `-` means stdin for reading or stdout for writing. Prefer
  `with click.open_file(path, mode) as f:`: its standard-stream wrapper prevents
  closure on context exit, not on an explicit forwarded `close()` call.
  [Tests](tests/test_utils.py#L471) cover regular files, `-`, and `Path("-")`.
- `atomic=True` writes beside the destination and replaces it on close; ordinary
  files require `w` mode (not `a` or `x`), and standard streams ignore atomic mode
  ([`open_stream`](src/click/_compat.py#L371)). This is **not rollback on error**:
  [`_AtomicFile.close`](src/click/_compat.py#L452) replaces even when its context
  exits with an exception. [Permission tests](tests/test_utils.py#L547) are
  explicitly skipped on Windows; they do not establish cross-platform guarantees.

## Deployment unknowns and next changes

No consuming application, deployed Click/Python version, environment-variable
contract, launch command, host platform, filesystem, or deployment process was
supplied. Repository examples are not deployment configuration. Confirm those
details before translating these source facts into an operational change.

For future implementation work, preserve focused coverage of explicit versus
automatic environment flags (including empty/false values), prompt precedence,
child versus group resource ownership, separate runner streams, and cleanup on
normal/error/early exits. The linked tests are starting points, not a claim that
all these edge cases already have regression coverage.

# Click contributor handoff

Scope: environment flags, chained resources, prompts, test output, files, and
cleanup. Reviewed from source, documentation, and test assertions on 2026-09-27
at commit `b6c8e841138ac6fe48aafbfe8c145fd5b88dc8ac`.
[Metadata](pyproject.toml) declares Click **8.2.1**, Python **>=3.10**.
These are repository facts, not a claim about an installed or deployed version.
No upstream code or tests were executed.

Start with the [README](README.md) and [documentation index](docs/index.rst).
This single handoff supplements their canonical material. Existing files remain
unchanged, including the README; this root file is the handoff entry point.

## Environment-driven flags

[Options guide](docs/options.md), [implementation](src/click/core.py)
(`Parameter.consume_value`, `Parameter.resolve_envvar_value`,
`Option.resolve_envvar_value`, `Option.get_default`):

- Value precedence is command line, environment, `default_map`, parameter default.
  Explicit `envvar` names are tried before automatic names. A list selects the
  first **nonempty** value; empty strings behave as absent, not as false.
- At this pin, an explicit nonempty `envvar` on a flag with a **truthy**
  `flag_value` substitutes `str(flag_value)` before type conversion. Thus an
  ordinary `is_flag=True` option with `envvar="FEATURE"` activates even for
  `FEATURE=false`, `0`, or arbitrary text. This is not boolean parsing of the
  environment text. The false/zero cases follow from implementation; the
  [test](tests/test_arguments.py) `test_envvar_flag_value` checks arbitrary text
  with `flag_value="upper"`.
- Automatic prefix lookup returns the raw environment value; falsey
  `flag_value` also bypasses substitution. When raw text reaches
  [BoolParamType.convert](src/click/types.py), it strips whitespace and ignores
  case: `1/true/t/yes/y/on` are true, `0/false/f/no/n/off` false; other text errors.
  Do not generalize the changelog's “always” substitution statement to these
  branches. Automatic prefixes include subcommand names, uppercase names, and
  normalize hyphens to underscores.
- For nonboolean flag groups sharing a destination, a truthy parameter default
  selects that flag's `flag_value`; `default=True` does not deliver boolean True.
  Type inference uses `flag_value` unless a type was supplied.

[Option tests](tests/test_options.py): `test_empty_envvar`,
`test_trailing_blanks_boolean_envvar`, `test_show_envvar_auto_prefix_dash_in_command`,
`test_type_from_flag_value`, and `test_flag_value_is_correctly_set`.
[Release notes](CHANGES.rst) identify the explicit-envvar change in 8.2 and the
typed-flag fix in 8.2.1. Preserve these distinctions when comparing versions.

## Chained-command resource lifetimes

[Command pipelines](docs/commands.rst) and `Group.invoke` in
[core](src/click/core.py) establish that a chained result callback receives the
ordered list of subcommand returns plus group parameters. Each subcommand's
context exits before that callback, but the group context remains active through
it. A returned processor must not depend on an already-open subcommand-owned
`click.File`; a **group-owned** file remains available. The guide's broad warning
about closed files must be read with this ownership distinction.

Use a group resource registered with `ctx.with_resource(...)`, or open a path
inside the result callback and finish consuming the pipeline before leaving its
`with` block. Simply calling `open_file` does not register context cleanup.
The guide's pipeline snippet also says `for x in input`; its declared argument
is `fin`. Follow [test_pipeline](tests/test_chain.py), which iterates its file
parameter `f`, and the implementation for lifetime ordering.

Chaining constraints: no nested groups; only the last command can have
`nargs=-1`; options precede arguments within each command. With
`invoke_without_command=True`, an empty chain passes `[]` to the result callback
(`test_no_command_result_callback` in the same test file).

## Interactive defaults

[Prompts guide](docs/prompts.rst) and `Option.consume_value` /
`prompt_for_value` in [core](src/click/core.py): an environment or `default_map`
value bypasses automatic prompting. To offer an editable environment-derived
default, use `prompt=True, default=lambda: os.environ.get("USER", "")`; a
higher-precedence value still bypasses the prompt. `show_default="current user"`
describes the callable in help without exposing its representation.

`prompt_required=False` prompts on a bare option, uses a supplied value directly,
and otherwise uses the default without prompting. `required=True` also prompts
when omitted. Ordinary `prompt=True` alone does not make a bare value-taking
option valid. Since 8.2, `show_default=False` hides the prompt's displayed default
without removing its value. See [option tests](tests/test_options.py)
`test_dynamic_default_help_text` and [terminal tests](tests/test_termui.py)
`test_prompt_required_with_required`, `test_prompt_required_false`, and
`test_false_show_default_cause_no_default_display_in_prompt`.

## CliRunner output compatibility

In 8.2+, `Result.output` is the mixed terminal stream in captured write order;
`stdout` and `stderr` stay separate, and empty stderr is `""`. `mix_stderr` was
removed. Choose `stdout` for payload assertions, `stderr` for diagnostics, and
`output` for the combined interaction. Text properties decode with replacement
and normalize CRLF; use the corresponding `*_bytes` for byte assertions.
8.2.1 flushes stderr at invocation end, including buffered writes.

Evidence: [Result and CliRunner.invoke](src/click/testing.py),
[test_stderr and test_isolation_flushes_unflushed_stderr](tests/test_testing.py),
[release notes](CHANGES.rst). The [testing guide](docs/testing.md) also explains
prompt input echo and filesystem isolation. CliRunner changes interpreter state
and is not thread-safe. Its “Context Settings” example asserts a debug message
that its displayed command never emits; do not copy that assertion.

## File opening and cleanup

[File guide](docs/handling-files.rst), [File implementation](src/click/types.py),
and [open_file / LazyFile](src/click/utils.py):

- `File` opens reads and standard streams immediately by default. Precisely,
  automatic laziness applies to modes containing `w`, not every writing mode
  (such as `a` or `x`). Explicit lazy reads still briefly open for validation.
  Deferred opening can raise `FileError` on access.
- `open_file` defaults to `lazy=False`, unlike `File("w")`. Manage its lifetime
  explicitly. `-` selects stdin/stdout; its context-manager wrapper avoids
  closing the standard stream. `File` registers close or flush with its context;
  conversion without a context leaves ownership to the caller. Already-file-like
  inputs are returned unchanged without registering cleanup.
- Atomic output writes to a sibling temporary file and replaces the destination
  on close, not flush. It requires `w` mode, rejects `a`/`x`, and is ignored for
  standard streams. At this pin, `_AtomicFile.close` ignores its `delete`
  argument and replaces even on exceptional context exit: do not assume rollback.
  See [open_stream / _AtomicFile](src/click/_compat.py),
  [test_file_atomics](tests/test_arguments.py), and
  [file opening and permission tests](tests/test_utils.py).

[Resource guide](docs/advanced.rst) and [Context implementation](src/click/core.py)
(`with_resource`, `call_on_close`, `close`, `__exit__`, `exit`) use an ExitStack:
resources/callbacks unwind in reverse registration order. Cleanup occurs before
the current context is popped. Since 8.2, `ctx.exit()` explicitly closes before
raising `Exit`; ordinary context teardown also closes. `close()` resets the
stack. Nested scopes defer cleanup; `scope(cleanup=False)` requires later cleanup.
Because teardown calls `ExitStack.close()` rather than forwarding the command's
exception, resource managers should not rely on receiving that exception.
Evidence: [context tests](tests/test_context.py), especially
`test_close_before_pop`, `test_close_before_exit`, and `test_with_resource`.

## Remaining boundaries

No deployment, consuming application, installed version, environment values,
terminal, or filesystem configuration was supplied. Before applying this handoff
to an application, establish its actual Click version and resource ownership.
For future changes, the named tests are focused regression starting points;
code-derived edge cases above are not claims of test execution or exhaustive
coverage. No product changes or deployment decisions are proposed here.

# Contributor handoff: request lifetime and deployment boundaries

Scope: Flask **3.1.1**, supplied commit `68e21c0aa6d423a695e00bddcc6e3fef79c3822a`.
This is a source-based handoff, not a deployed application's runbook. Links point to
canonical files in this checkout; test names identify evidence to revisit. No code
or tests were run. [Package metadata](pyproject.toml) requires Python >=3.9,
Werkzeug >=3.1 and ItsDangerous >=2.2; these minimums do not establish a live
installation's versions. See the [release notes](CHANGES.rst) before backporting.

## Async and background work

- Coroutine routes, error handlers, request hooks and teardown functions are
  supported with the `async` extra (asgiref). Class-based views are supported too.
  `Flask.ensure_sync` leaves synchronous functions alone and wraps coroutine
  functions through asgiref; extension decorators should call it when invoking
  views. Existing blocking extension code does not become asynchronous.
- Under ordinary WSGI serving, an async view still occupies one worker per
  request. Awaiting concurrent I/O can help within that request; it does not
  increase the worker's request concurrency or accelerate CPU work.
- Do not rely on `asyncio.create_task` in an ordinary async view for background
  completion: unfinished tasks are cancelled when its event loop stops. Use a
  task queue for work that must outlive the request. The documented
  `WsgiToAsgi` adapter provides a continuing loop, but that alone is not durable
  job storage or a retry policy (operational inference).
- The Celery factory example wraps each task in `app.app_context()`, registers
  the Celery app in `app.extensions`, and uses `shared_task`. Pass serializable
  IDs/data, reconstruct resources in the task, return a task ID and poll rather
  than wait for the result inside the request. Its local Redis settings are
  examples, not deployment facts.

Evidence: [async guide](docs/async-await.rst), [adapter guide](docs/deploying/asgi.rst),
[`ensure_sync` / `async_to_sync`](src/flask/app.py),
[async tests](tests/test_async.py) (`test_async_route`, `test_async_error_handler`,
`test_async_before_after_request`), [Celery guide](docs/patterns/celery.rst),
[factory implementation](examples/celery/src/task_app/__init__.py).

## Proxy deployment

Use a production WSGI server or the documented ASGI adapter, not the development
server. Apply Werkzeug `ProxyFix` to `app.wsgi_app` only behind a trusted proxy.
Set trust counts **per forwarded header** according to the actual chain; the
example's `x_for=1, x_proto=1, x_host=1, x_prefix=1` is not a universal setting.
Different proxies may set different headers. Incorrect trust permits clients to
spoof address, scheme, host or mount-prefix information. ProxyFix belongs to
Werkzeug; its implementation is not present in this repository.

In 3.1, `SERVER_NAME` does **not** restrict incoming hosts. Use `TRUSTED_HOSTS`
(default `None`, accepting all hosts) for host validation: exact names or a
leading dot for subdomains; rejected hosts yield 400 during routing. Request
hooks still run. `SERVER_NAME` remains relevant to subdomain matching and URL
building outside requests. Configure the actual external scheme and mount path
when building URLs outside a request; forwarded request data is unavailable there.

Evidence: [production guide](docs/deploying/index.rst),
[proxy guide](docs/deploying/proxy_fix.rst), [configuration](docs/config.rst)
(`TRUSTED_HOSTS`, `SERVER_NAME`, `APPLICATION_ROOT`, `PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME`),
[`create_url_adapter`](src/flask/app.py),
[`test_trusted_hosts_config`](tests/test_request.py),
[URL generation tests](tests/test_appctx.py).

## Streaming responses

Return a synchronous iterator yielding strings/bytes, optionally with response
headers. An async view is supported; an async response iterator is not. The 3.1.1
Sans-IO `AsyncIterable` typing change is explicitly for Quart compatibility and
must not be interpreted as Flask runtime support.

Ordinary response iteration occurs after the view returns and loses request
context. Construct `stream_with_context` while a request is active if iteration
needs `request` or `session`; it accepts an iterator or decorates a generator
function. Template streaming automatically uses it when a request is active.
The wrapper retains context until exhaustion/close and closes an underlying
iterator with a `close` method. Consume or close streamed responses in future
tests; retained contexts can prolong resource lifetimes.

Set status, headers and session changes **before returning the response**.
`process_response` saves the session before body iteration; retaining session
access does not make changes during iteration persist in the response cookie.
Read session data in the view as well when it must influence `Vary: Cookie`.
The guide's “each yield ... directly sent to the browser” describes application
streaming, not a verified delivery guarantee: middleware and deployment buffering
can prevent incremental delivery. Validate that separately on the chosen stack.

Evidence: [streaming guide](docs/patterns/streaming.rst),
[`make_response` / `process_response`](src/flask/app.py),
[`stream_with_context`](src/flask/helpers.py), [`_stream`](src/flask/templating.py),
[`save_session`](src/flask/sessions.py), [3.1.1 notes](CHANGES.rst),
[streaming tests](tests/test_helpers.py) (`test_streaming_with_context`,
`test_streaming_with_context_and_custom_close`, `test_stream_keeps_session`),
[`test_client_pop_all_preserved`](tests/test_testing.py).

## Session-key rotation

For the built-in secure-cookie session, set the new signing key as `SECRET_KEY`
and retain accepted old keys in `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` (added in 3.1, default
`None`). Order old keys oldest to newest for efficient fallback checks. Remove
old keys after the application's chosen acceptance window; extensions or custom
session backends must be checked separately for rotation support.

**Use the 3.1.1 behavior as the baseline:** it fixes signing-key selection order.
`get_signing_serializer` puts fallback keys first and the current key last, so
new cookies use the current key. Fallbacks accept existing signatures; an
unverifiable cookie loads as an empty session. Rotation does not force every
cookie to be rewritten: `should_set_cookie` normally requires modification or a
permanent session with refresh enabled. Signature age is checked against
`PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME` when loading. Choose rollout overlap and retirement
accordingly; do not assume a universal rotation interval.

Evidence: [configuration](docs/config.rst) (`SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS`,
`PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME`, `SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST`),
[session implementation](src/flask/sessions.py),
[`test_session_secret_key_fallbacks` / `test_session_expiration`](tests/test_basic.py),
[3.1.0 and 3.1.1 notes](CHANGES.rst).

## Application-context resources

`current_app` and `g` require an application context. Requests and registered
Flask CLI commands push one automatically; independent jobs should use
`with app.app_context():`. That does not create an HTTP request or its session.
`g` is scoped to an application context, not persistent cross-request storage.
A manually retained outer context can outlive individual requests.

Follow the documented lazy-resource pattern: create once in `get_db`, cache on
`g`, then `g.pop('db', None)` and close it in `teardown_appcontext`. Cleanup must
handle resources never created and exception paths. Teardown occurs on the final
context pop; streaming can defer it. Do not pass context proxies or open database
connections as background-job arguments.

Evidence: [application context guide](docs/appcontext.rst),
[`AppContext` / `RequestContext`](src/flask/ctx.py),
[context tests](tests/test_appctx.py) (context availability, handled/unhandled
exceptions and `test_context_refcounts`), [task data guidance](docs/patterns/celery.rst).

## Request-size limits

| Config / request attribute | Default | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH` / `max_content_length` | `None` | Total request bytes read |
| `MAX_FORM_MEMORY_SIZE` / `max_form_memory_size` | `500_000` bytes | Non-file multipart field size |
| `MAX_FORM_PARTS` / `max_form_parts` | `1_000` | Multipart field count |

Exceeding a limit raises `RequestEntityTooLarge` (413) during reading/parsing.
Set overrides before any middleware/hook/view reads the body or parses form data.
These are not interchangeable file-upload limits or overall process-memory caps;
also assess proxy/server limits and timeouts. With no content-length limit, no
`Content-Length` and no server indication that the stream terminates, no data is
read to avoid an unbounded stream.

3.1 added per-request content-length overrides and Flask configuration for the
form limits. Two source-specific corrections matter:

- The config guide's `Request.max_form_memory_parts` reference is a typo; the
  implementation and tests use **`request.max_form_memory_size`**.
- Although the property prose describes `None` as unlimited, these getters treat
  a per-request `None` as “fall back to app config” (or Werkzeug defaults outside
  app context). Assigning `request.max_content_length = None` does not disable a
  finite app limit; the same sentinel behavior applies to the form properties.

The security guide's 500 MB calculation is a field-count × field-size estimate,
not an aggregate memory guarantee covering files, parser overhead or concurrency.
The checked-in tests cover config/default/override precedence and a form-triggered
413 handler; they do not establish behavior through a live proxy or every parser
edge case. Parsing is delegated to Werkzeug.

Evidence: [configuration](docs/config.rst), [resource guidance](docs/web-security.rst),
[request properties](src/flask/wrappers.py), [defaults](src/flask/app.py),
[`test_limit_config` / `test_max_content_length`](tests/test_request.py).

## Unknown deployment details to establish before rollout

No live topology or application configuration was supplied. A future contributor
must establish the server/worker model and installed versions; proxy chain and
header sanitization; external host/scheme/prefix; buffering, disconnect handling
and timeouts; body limits at each layer; queue/broker, retry and result-retention
policy; extension async/rotation compatibility; and the key rollout/retirement
window across all instances. These are open operational decisions, not settings
inferred from examples. Verify streaming delivery and cleanup, old/new-cookie
acceptance, host rejection and size-limit responses on that actual stack.

# Contributor handoff: request and worker lifetimes

Start with the [project README](README.md) and [documentation index](docs/index.rst).
This is a focused source handoff for Flask, a WSGI framework, at commit
`68e21c0aa6d423a695e00bddcc6e3fef79c3822a`. The [package metadata](pyproject.toml)
declares **3.1.1**, Python >=3.9, Werkzeug >=3.1 and ItsDangerous >=2.2.
Facts below were reviewed against repository docs, implementation and test source
on 2026-09-27; tests were read, not executed. They do not establish a deployed
application's configuration. This single entry point supplements the existing
documentation; existing files are intentionally unchanged.

## Async views and background work

- Coroutine routes, class-based views, error handlers and request/teardown hooks
  are supported with the `async` extra. `Flask.ensure_sync` delegates coroutine
  functions to asgiref; without it, calling an async view raises a runtime error.
  Extension decorators must also call `ensure_sync` appropriately; synchronous
  extension operations can still block.
- Under ordinary WSGI handling, an async view still occupies one worker for the
  request. It enables concurrent I/O within that view, not extra request capacity
  or faster CPU work. Unfinished tasks spawned in its temporary event loop are
  cancelled when the view completes: `asyncio.create_task` is not a durable job
  mechanism.
- The documented background-work pattern is a task queue. The Celery example
  wraps task execution in `with app.app_context()`, initializes through the app
  factory, and uses `shared_task`. Pass serializable IDs/data and reacquire
  resources in the task. Return a task ID and poll rather than waiting for the
  result in the request. A worker must run separately; the example's Redis URLs
  are examples, not deployment evidence.
- The documented ASGI alternative wraps Flask with `asgiref.wsgi.WsgiToAsgi` and
  serves the wrapper. Its continuing loop permits spawned asyncio tasks, but
  does not establish persistence across process loss or queue delivery guarantees.

## Proxy deployment

Use a production server; the development server is not a production option.
`ProxyFix` wraps `app.wsgi_app` only when there really is a trusted proxy in front.
Configure trusted hop counts **separately for each forwarded header**. The guide's
`x_for=1, x_proto=1, x_host=1, x_prefix=1` is illustrative, not a safe universal
configuration: clients can forge headers and proxies do not all set the same ones.
Werkzeug supplies the middleware; this checkout does not contain its implementation.

In 3.1, `SERVER_NAME` no longer restricts incoming hosts. Use `TRUSTED_HOSTS`
for host validation (default `None`, allowing all hosts); invalid hosts yield 400
during routing, and before/after-request callbacks still run. Outside requests,
URL generation instead needs `SERVER_NAME`, with `APPLICATION_ROOT` and
`PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME` describing the intended external URL. These are not proof
of actual proxy routing, TLS or mount paths.

## Streaming responses

Return a synchronous iterator yielding strings/bytes, optionally with response
headers. Ordinary request context is unavailable during later iteration; create
`stream_with_context` while a request is active if the generator needs `request`
or `session`. Template streaming applies this wrapper automatically when a
request is active. The wrapper retains context until exhaustion/close and closes
the underlying iterator; long streams can therefore retain context resources.

Set headers and make session changes before returning the response. Session
saving happens in `process_response`, before body iteration; keeping the session
readable in a generator does not make later mutations persist to a cookie.
Middleware and proxy buffering can prevent prompt client delivery, so the
streaming guide's “directly sent to the browser” is not an end-to-end guarantee.

**3.1.1 typing pitfall:** the sans-io base allows `AsyncIterable` for Quart's
typing needs. Flask's runtime does not thereby support async-generator response
bodies; `make_response` handles synchronous iterators.

## Session-key rotation

`SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` (added in 3.1, default `None`) lets the built-in secure
cookie session read cookies signed with retained old keys. Keep the current key
in `SECRET_KEY`; 3.1.1 constructs the serializer with fallbacks followed by that
key so newly saved cookies use the current key. **3.1.0 had a signing-key selection
bug fixed in 3.1.1**; do not assume identical rotation behavior across those versions.
Fallbacks do not replace a missing current key.

The config guide recommends oldest-to-newest fallbacks for verification efficiency.
Its “last key first” wording concerns verification, not selecting an old key for
new signatures. The rotation regression test writes with an initial key, observes
an empty session after replacing it, then recovers the cookie with that original
key as a fallback. Invalid/expired signatures produce an empty session; fallback
keys do not bypass the `PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME` signature-age check.

Retire old keys after an application-specific overlap period; every retained key
adds verification work. Reading an old cookie alone does not guarantee reissuance:
normal session save/refresh rules still apply. Extensions and custom session
interfaces must be checked independently for fallback support.

[`SecureCookieSessionInterface` and `should_set_cookie`](src/flask/sessions.py),

## Application-context resources

`g` belongs to an application context, not to the process and not to a user across
requests. Requests and registered Flask CLI commands push an app context;
standalone/background activity can explicitly use `with app.app_context()`.
An app context alone does not provide a request or session.

Cache a resource lazily on `g`; register `teardown_appcontext` to pop and close it
if present. Teardown must tolerate partial initialization and runs on context
exit, including exceptional exit. An explicitly extended context (including a
stream) can outlive the usual request lifetime. The tutorial's database test
checks same-context reuse and closure after exit.

Evidence: [app-context guide](docs/appcontext.rst), [context push/pop](src/flask/ctx.py),
[context and teardown tests](tests/test_appctx.py),
[database resource pattern](examples/tutorial/flaskr/db.py),

## Request-size limits

| App config | Default | Request override | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH` | `None` | `request.max_content_length` | Total request bytes read |
| `MAX_FORM_MEMORY_SIZE` | `500_000` | `request.max_form_memory_size` | Non-file multipart field bytes |
| `MAX_FORM_PARTS` | `1_000` | `request.max_form_parts` | Multipart part count |

Exceeding a limit during reading/parsing raises 413. Set overrides before any
body/form access, including access by hooks. Per-request content-length overrides
and the two form config keys were added in 3.1. With no content-length limit,
no `Content-Length` header and no server indication of a terminated input stream,
no body is read to avoid an infinite stream.

**Resolve the config-guide typo:** `Request.max_form_memory_parts` does not exist;
the implementation and `test_limit_config` establish `max_form_memory_size`.
Also, assigning `None` to any of these request properties clears its override and
falls back to app config in this version; it does not disable a configured limit.
App-level `None` is the documented way to omit a limit. Form limits do not replace
a total upload limit or server/proxy resource controls. The security guide's
500 MB field-size arithmetic is not a bound on total process memory or file uploads.

Evidence: [configuration reference](docs/config.rst),
[resource-use guidance](docs/web-security.rst),
[request getters/setters](src/flask/wrappers.py), [app defaults](src/flask/app.py),
[`test_limit_config` and 413 handling test](tests/test_request.py).
Parsing itself is delegated to Werkzeug; these Flask tests do not establish

## Deployment unknowns and next checks

No live deployment details were supplied. Before applying this handoff to an app,
establish its installed dependency versions and extension compatibility; server
and worker model; proxy chain, header sanitization and trust counts; external host,
scheme and path; streaming buffering/timeouts; queue broker, workers and delivery
requirements; session interface, rollout overlap and key-retirement policy; and
body limits at every ingress layer. Use configuration and authorized deployment
evidence to answer these. Repository examples establish none of those choices.
